blocks.text: But something else comes to mind, on which I should like the learned to judge. Among the Arabs ديك [dīk] dik is a cock, and ديكة [dīka] dika is a hen. Hence there is a not insubstantial conjecture that among the Hebrews too, or the Syrians, דיך dik, or דוך duk, signified a cock, and דוך כפא duk kepha a cock of the rock. When these words coalesced into one κατὰ σύνθεσιν [kata synthesin], I suspect that from duk-kepha, by a slight change, דוכיפת dukiphath was formed, one of the two Caphs being dropped; its absence could not be supplied by the point Daghes because of the long vowel preceding. The teachers of the Hebrews, who could not have thought of such a composition, since they did not know that duk or dik is a cock, nevertheless strongly confirm our conjecture when they explain dukiphath as the field cock, or the wild cock, or the mountain cock. And almost all the more recent writers explain it so. Kimchi and Aquinas render it תרנגולא ברא, field cock. R. Serira Gaon, גאלו דמונ״טייא, cock of the mountains. Pomarius, תרנגול הבר, cock of the field, and in Italian gallo, o gallina salvatica. Elias Levita in German אוירהאן awerhan, which is a kind of wild cock. The Syriac too has here ܬܪܢܓܠܐ ܕܒܪܐ, field cock. And the three Chaldees, the Jerusalem, Jonathan and Onkelos, נגר טורא, mountain cock. The field cock, moreover, or mountain cock, is (I believe) the same as the rock-dwelling cock; especially since mountain and rock are so far synonymous that the Elders use them interchangeably: hence they render the Hebrew צור in some places πέτραν [petran], rock, in others ὄρος [oros], mountain.

Although I think this is the true origin of the word, nevertheless another explanation of this composition can also be given [col. 345], and a fairly probable one. Namely, if the word דוכיפת is split into דוך and יפת, the former being cock, the latter to portend. For from it comes מופת, a sign, not of any kind, says Kimchi, but one by which something future is portended. Taken in this way as דוך־יפת, it will be the portentous cock, or even the ominous cock, or the augural cock ^{(1)}.

[III, 109] Now we must see to which bird above all these names can be assigned. There are four interpretations. One is that of the Sadducees, who, understanding by the name דוכיפת the common hen, abstained from eating it as an unclean bird forbidden in the Law. To this belongs Aben Ezra's sarcasm against them: אמרו הצדוקים שהיא תרנגולת ואלה טפשי עולם כי מי הגיד להם, The Sadducees said that dukiphath is the hen. But these are the fools of the world (that is, the most foolish of mortals). For who told them this? The second is the interpretation of Elias in the Methurgeman, where he says that נגר טורא is called in German אוריארה״אן awerhan, or orhan. That is a kind of wild cock, twice as large as the common one. Gesner thinks it is Pliny's tetrao. He himself, following Albertus, calls it urogallus, a Latin name coined on the model of the German. They think it is so called from the uri [aurochs], because it exceeds common cocks in size as much as the aurochs exceed common oxen. The third interpretation is that of Junius and Tremellius, for whom דוכיפת is the attagen, a bird that was among the chief delicacies of the ancients. Horace, Epode 2:
May no African bird descend into my belly, no Ionian attagen.
Among the flavours of birds the first is said to be the taste of Ionian attagens.
The Greeks call them ἀτταγᾶς [attagas] and ἀτταγῆνας [attagēnas] ^{a)}. Aristophanes in the Storks:
Ἀτταγᾶς, ἥδιστον ἑψεῖν ἐν ἐπινικίοις κρέας. [Attagas, hēdiston hepsein en epinikiois kreas.]
[III, 110] Phoenicides ἐν Μισουμένῃ [en Misoumenē], after a long list of dainties:
— — κ᾽ οὐδὲν ἦν τούτων ὅλως — [k᾽ ouden ēn toutōn holōs —] Πρὸς τὸν ἀταγῆνα συμβαλεῖν τῶν βρωμάτων. [Pros ton atagēna symbalein tōn brōmatōn.]

But the description of so delicate a bird has been so neglected that today the learned dispute whether the attagen is the gallinago [snipe], or the rusticula [woodcock], or the coturnix [quail], or the francolinus of the Italians. By Junius it seems to be taken for the rusticula, which is called woodcock, that is, wild cock, and in some places by the French gelinotte de bois, that is, little wild hen.
